scenes.heading: Electrolysis
scenes.sub: Using electricity to force a reaction uphill
scenes.say: Electrolysis uses electricity to force a redox reaction that wouldn't happen on its own. It's how aluminium and chlorine are made, how copper is purified, and what happens when your phone battery charges.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Riding downhill is easy; pushing the bike back up takes effort
scenes.science: A power supply forces a non-spontaneous reaction to happen
scenes.breaks: a bike just stores energy as height; electrolysis makes new substances, and some energy is always lost as heat.
scenes.say: A galvanic cell is like riding a bike downhill: the reaction goes by itself. An electrolytic cell is like pushing it back up. The reaction is non-spontaneous, so a power supply has to keep pushing electrons to make it happen.

scenes.heading: Galvanic vs electrolytic

left.title: Galvanic cell
points: Two half-cells and a salt bridge

scenes.say: In both cells, oxidation is at the anode and reduction is at the cathode: an ox, red cat. What flips is the polarity. For an electrolytic cell, remember PANIC: positive anode, negative is cathode.

scenes.heading: Predicting the products
points: Water is reduced before Na⁺ and K⁺
Na and Al need a molten electrolyte
scenes.say: List every species, including water and the electrode. At the cathode, the strongest oxidant is reduced; at the anode, the strongest reductant is oxidised. In solution, water reacts before sodium or potassium ions, so those metals need a molten electrolyte.

scenes.heading: Faraday's laws
scenes.equation: Q = I × t   n(e⁻) = Q ÷ F
scenes.say: Faraday's laws link charge to amount. Charge, Q, equals current times time, with time in seconds. Divide by the Faraday constant, ninety-six thousand five hundred coulombs per mole, to get moles of electrons. Then use the half-equation ratio.
scenes.caption: Faraday's laws link charge to amount. Q = I × t, with time in seconds. Divide by the Faraday constant, 96 500 C mol⁻¹, to get moles of electrons. Then use the half-equation ratio.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 2.00 A passes through CuSO₄ solution for 30.0 minutes. What mass of copper is deposited? (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu)
scenes.say: Convert thirty minutes to eighteen hundred seconds. The charge is thirty-six hundred coulombs. Divide by the Faraday constant: zero point zero three seven three one moles of electrons. Copper needs two electrons each, so halve it, then multiply by sixty-three point five. That's one point one eight grams.
scenes.caption: Convert 30.0 minutes to 1800 s. The charge is 3600 C. Divide by F: 0.03731 mol of electrons. Copper needs two electrons each, so halve it, then multiply by 63.5. That's 1.18 g.

scenes.heading: Electrolysis in industry
scenes.say: Industry relies on this. Aluminium comes from aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. Chlorine comes from concentrated brine. In electroplating, the object you're coating is the cathode. And in copper refining, an active copper anode dissolves.

points: An Ox, Red Cat: true in every cell
Strongest oxidant reduced at the cathode
Water reacts before Na⁺ and K⁺
scenes.say: Quick recap. Oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode. In electrolysis, the anode is positive. The strongest oxidant is reduced and the strongest reductant is oxidised. And always use seconds in Q equals I t. Now try the practice questions!
